content: Pellagra is a disease caused by a deficiency of niacin (vitamin B3) and protein, particularly proteins containing the essential amino acid tryptophan. Tryptophan can be converted into niacin in the body, so foods rich in tryptophan, such as milk, can prevent pellagra even if they lack niacin. However, if dietary tryptophan is primarily used for protein synthesis, niacin deficiency may still occur. Tryptophan is found in high concentrations in foods like meat, poultry, fish, and eggs. Consuming these foods reduces the need for niacin from other dietary sources. The relationship between lysine and pellagra remains unclear. Historically, traditional food preparation methods, such as nixtamalization (treating corn with lime, an alkali), used by native New World cultivators who domesticated corn, made niacin nutritionally available and reduced the risk of pellagra. When corn cultivation spread globally, this preparation method was not widely adopted because its benefits were not understood. Consequently, populations heavily reliant on untreated corn as a staple food began to suffer from pellagra. Native cultivators who used nixtamalization did not experience the disease. Pellagra was first described in Spain in 1735 by Gaspar Casal, who published a clinical description in his posthumous work Natural and Medical History of the Asturian Principality (1762). The disease was initially referred to as Asturian leprosy and is recognized as the first modern pathological description of a syndrome. In northern Italy, where the disease was endemic, Francesco Frapoli of Milan named it pelle agra (meaning rough skin). For centuries, outbreaks of pellagra in regions where maize was a dominant food crop led to the belief that maize either carried a toxic substance or was a carrier of disease. It was only later, upon observing the absence of pellagra outbreaks in Mesoamerica (where maize was processed traditionally), that the role of dietary factors, rather than toxins, was considered. In the early 1900s, pellagra reached epidemic proportions in the American South. In 1915, South Carolina reported 1,306 pellagra-related deaths within the first ten months, and by 1916, 100,000 Southerners were affected. At the time, the scientific community believed pellagra was caused by a germ or an unknown toxin in corn. The Spartanburg Pellagra Hospital in South Carolina was the first facility in the United States dedicated to researching the disease. In 1915, Joseph Goldberger, assigned by the U.S. Surgeon General to study pellagra, demonstrated that the disease was linked to diet by inducing it in prisoners. By 1926, Goldberger established that a balanced diet or a small amount of baker's yeast could prevent pellagra. Despite his findings, skepticism persisted in the medical community until 1937, when Conrad Elvehjem showed that niacin cured pellagra (manifested as black tongue in dogs). Subsequent studies by Tom Spies, Marion Blankenhorn, and Clark Cooper confirmed that niacin also cured pellagra in humans, earning them recognition as Time Magazine's 1938 Men of the Year in comprehensive science. Pellagra is most common in populations that derive most of their caloric intake from maize, as untreated corn is a poor source of niacin and tryptophan. This disease is prevalent in rural South America, where corn is a dietary staple. Symptoms often appear in the spring, worsen during the summer due to increased sun exposure, and reappear the following spring. Pellagra was also common in the American South, particularly in states like Mississippi and Alabama, and among inmates in jails and orphanages. Joseph Goldberger studied the disease in a penal colony in Rankin. Alkali treatment of corn corrects niacin deficiency and was a common practice in Native American cultures that cultivated corn. Protein deficiencies must be balanced by consuming other protein sources. Pellagra was also observed among prisoners in Soviet labor camps (Gulags) and in cases of chronic alcoholism. The symptoms of pellagra include high sensitivity to sunlight, aggression, dermatitis, smooth and beefy red glossitis, red skin lesions, insomnia, weakness, mental confusion, diarrhea, and eventually dementia. The primary manifestations of pellagra can be remembered as the four D's: diarrhea, dermatitis, dementia, and death.
